name: Apollo 16’s third stage
intro: This crater was made by the third stage of the Saturn V that launched Apollo 16. It crashed on 19 April 1972, but its radio stopped working before impact, so for more than 40 years nobody knew exactly where. Cameras on NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter finally found it in 2015. Look up: the see-through rocket stage over the crater shows how it looked a moment before it hit.

hotspots.title: The lost crater
hotspots.text: The crater is oval, about 40 by 30 meters, with a mound in the middle. It lies about 30 km from where Apollo-era trackers guessed.

source.label: LROC: Found! Apollo 16 S-IVB impact crater

photo.alt: A grey moonscape seen from above with a fresh crater and dark and bright streaks around it.
photo.caption: The crater found in LRO images in 2015.
photo.licenseEvidence: LRO camera (LROC) image from NASA GSFC’s archive. LROC images (NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University) are used here for education with credit, as the team agreed.

hotspots.title: One big engine
hotspots.text: This is the stage’s single J-2 engine. It burned liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen to push the Apollo ships out of Earth orbit and onto the road to the Moon.

hotspots.title: Mostly fuel tank
hotspots.text: Nearly all of the stage is fuel tank: 17.8 meters tall and 6.6 meters across, about as tall as a six-storey building. By the time it reached the Moon its fuel was used up.

hotspots.title: Open at the top
hotspots.text: The lunar module rode to space folded up inside the top of this stage, with the command ship above it. Once the crew had pulled the lander out and flown on, the top was left open.

hotspots.title: Long rays
hotspots.text: Streaks of thrown-out soil stretch hundreds of meters from the rim.

source.label: LROC: Found! Apollo 16 S-IVB impact crater

hotspots.title: Lost contact
hotspots.text: Scout’s check: the stage’s radio fell silent before the crash, so its timing had to be worked out later from seismometer readings.

source.label: NSSDCA: Apollo impact sites on the Moon

hotspots.title: Found at last
hotspots.text: In December 2015 the LRO camera team announced that they had found the crater, in Mare Insularum.

source.label: LROC: Found! Apollo 16 S-IVB impact crater

funFact: It was lost on the Moon for more than 40 years, until a scientist spotted its crater in LRO pictures.
whyLeft: It was used up after sending Apollo 16 on its way, so NASA aimed it at the Moon as a giant test thump for the seismometers.
repurpose: It shattered on impact. Like the other stages, its aluminium fragments could one day be gathered by a Moon base.

source.label: LROC: Apollo 16 S-IVB crater found, 40 x 30 m (depth 2-3 m: Plescia et al. 2016)
